title: Elon Musk says Trump is 'ultimately' responsible for any curbs on Ukraine's Starshield systems
description: SpaceX CEO Elon Musk attends a meeting with US President Donald Trump and technology executives about artificial intelligence in the East Room of the
body: SpaceX CEO Elon Musk attends a meeting with US President Donald Trump and technology executives about artificial intelligence in the East Room of the White House in Washington, DC, on Sept. 29, 2026. Kent Nishimura | AFP | Getty ImagesSpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk said Wednesday that the U.S. government and President Donald Trump was responsible for any curbs on Ukraine's military-grade Starlink network.Writing on X, Musk said that "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the U.S. government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS."Ukraine had accused SpaceX of imposing new restrictions on the Starshield internet service without warning, leading to disruptions to Ukrainian military operations amid fresh Russian strikes on its energy infrastructure. On Wednesday, Serhii Beskrestnov, an advisor to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on defense technology, said SpaceX had implemented a speed limit on Starlink terminals in motion, without notifying the country's defense forces. That had disrupted some missions, and the same restrictions also applied to Starshield, he said on Telegram. Starlink is used to operate Ukraine's interceptor drones, the "most effective solution" against Moscow's Shahed drones, Beskrestnov said. Starshield is a military-grade satellite network, while Starlink is only meant for "civilian or defensive activities," Musk said. Some restrictions appear to have been partially lifted, with former Ukrainian defense minister Mykhailo Fedorov thanking Musk early Thursday morning that Starlink connectivity at speeds of up to 160 kilometers an hour had been restored. "Removing Starshield's speed limit entirely is now critical for Ukraine's defense," Fedorov added. The developments come amid tensions between Kyiv and Washington over an "energy ceasefire," between Ukraine and Russia announced by U.S. President Donald Trump. Ukraine has, however, welcomed a deal subject to Moscow honoring its commitment, while Russian authorities said talks were ongoing, without confirming whether they had reached an agreement. On Monday, Zelenskyy accused the Russians of breaching the ceasefire. Trump had also taken aim at Ukraine as it continues to strike Russian energy facilities, saying that Kyiv's attacks were responsible for the increase in diesel prices, instead of the U.S.' war with Iran. Washington has threatened to cut intelligence sharing with Kyiv, Reuters reported Wednesday, while Ukrainian officials said a day earlier that they have not received warnings of Russian attacks on the country for two straight days.— CNBC's Elsa Olhen contributed to this report.

schema.headline: Elon Musk says Trump is 'ultimately' responsible for any curbs on Ukraine's Starshield systems

title: Meta- and Google-backed Jio Platforms to raise up to $3.2 billion in historic IPO in India
description: NEW DELHI, INDIA - 2026/10/09: A security guard talks on his phone near the Jio logo, (representing Reliance Jio Infocomm Limited, a telecommunication
body: NEW DELHI, INDIA - 2026/10/09: A security guard talks on his phone near the Jio logo, (representing Reliance Jio Infocomm Limited, a telecommunications and digital services provider in India).Sopa Images | Lightrocket | Getty ImagesMeta- and Google-backed Jio Platforms, India's largest telecom operator, is looking to raise up to 302 billion rupees ($3.2 billion) through an initial public offering of shares.Jio Platforms will sell 270 million shares in IPO priced between 1,065 rupees and 1,119 rupees apiece,  from Oct. 21 to Oct. 23. Reliance Industries, the parent company of the telecom operator, said in an exchange filing.The share sale will be India's largest ever in rupee terms, but the second largest in dollar terms, marginally trailing the Hyundai Motors IPO that raised $3.3 billion in 2024. As per estimates provided by Indian market intelligence firm Prime Database, Jio was expected to raise around 377 billion rupees through its IPO.At the top end of the price range, Jio Platforms is valued at around $108 billion, much lower than previously expected. While Jio Platforms has been positioning itself as a tech company and not just a traditional utility provider, investors seem unconvinced.Jio Platforms, at its core, is a telecom company, Deven Choksey, managing director of Mumbai-based DRChoksey Finserv, told CNBC. While entertainment or gaming applications owned by Jio Platforms increase data consumption, the company earns revenues primarily from selling internet data, he added.Jio is the largest telecom company in India with over half a million subscribers, but at its current price it will be valued less than Bharti Airtel, the second largest player in the country. Bharti Airtel has a market cap of $117.5 billion, as per LSEG data.Indian billionaire Mukesh Ambani's flagship company, Reliance Industries, owns more than a 66% stake in Jio Platforms, followed by Meta Platforms' affiliate Jaadhu Holdings that owns nearly 10% and Google International, which owns 7.7%, as per LSEG data.Neither Meta nor Google will sell their stake in the company, according to the IPO papers.Jio Platforms also plans to roll out satellite communications services in India, putting it at the center of the spat between owner Ambani and Starlink's Elon Musk. Jio is reportedly looking to set up a network of around 1,600 LEO satellites and 23 ground stations to expand connectivity across India.Musk, last Saturday, accused Ambani of blocking Starlink's launch in India to maintain his "monopolistic exploitation" of the Indian market.

schema.headline: Meta- and Google-backed Jio Platforms to raise up to $3.2 billion in historic IPO in India

title: Oil falls as investors assess Mideast tensions, International Energy Agency's report
description: A vessel transits the Gulf of Oman off the coast of Khor Fakkan in the emirate of Sharjah in the east of the UAE on October 13, 2026. - | Afp | Getty
body: A vessel transits the Gulf of Oman off the coast of Khor Fakkan in the emirate of Sharjah in the east of the UAE on October 13, 2026. - | Afp | Getty ImagesOil fell Thursday as traders assessed potential supply disruptions following attacks on ships passing through the Strait of Hormuz, while digesting the International Energy Agency's latest monthly report on the outlook of the oil market.Futures for international benchmark Brent crude for December delivery dropped 1.66% to $104.31 a barrel. U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures for November fell 1.09% to $94.05 per barrel.Stock Chart IconStock chart icon brentA Singapore registered ship was sunk in the critical Strait of Hormuz, which raised worries of a prolonged Mideast conflict. "Such attacks are unprovoked, unjustifiable and a breach of international law," the Singapore maritime authority said in a statement Wednesday. Iran, meanwhile, has said it is "counting the moments" until it can start striking U.S. warships. The International Energy Agency in its oil report for October out Wednesday cautioned that constraints on diesel markets could continue well into the next year, with fresh attacks on Saudi Arabia threatening to derail a recovery in oil supply. To help ease prices, the Trump administration is considering to ease sanctions on "shadow fleet" vessels which transports ​oil and petroleum products from countries such as Russia, Reuters reported. Stock Chart IconStock chart icon wtiThe lack of progress between U.S.-Iran diplomatic track "leaves little immediate prospect of a full reopening of the waterway," said Firas Bechwaty, head of business development at online trading platform ICM late Wednesday. "At the same time, Saudi crude continues to reach international buyers through alternative routes, while accelerated emergency stock releases by IEA members provide an additional buffer, preventing a sharp rise in prices, even as tensions remain elevated,"  Bechwaty noted.

schema.headline: Oil falls as investors assess Mideast tensions, International Energy Agency's report

title: Bank of America hired 1,000 contractors to patch software flaws exposed by Anthropic's Mythos
description: watch nowBank of America has hired an army of external contractors to help it patch software vulnerabilities exposed by advanced artificial intelligen
body: watch nowBank of America has hired an army of external contractors to help it patch software vulnerabilities exposed by advanced artificial intelligence models including Anthropic's Mythos, the bank's CEO, Brian Moynihan, told CNBC on Wednesday.In an interview after the bank's third-quarter earnings release, Moynihan said that earlier this year the company rushed to bolster a wide spectrum of its internal and vendor code using thousands of employees and outside personnel. "That risk is real risk, and that's why when the frontier-type models came out. … A lot of us sat down and said, 'How do we figure out how to get through this quickly?" Moynihan told CNBC's Leslie Picker."We put on 1,000 contractors to help us do the patching work in the second quarter, and those people remain here today, helping us, on top of the 3,000 people we have in that area," he said.The bank spent a "couple hundred million plus" on the software remediation and regulatory issues related to anti-money laundering compliance in the third quarter, Moynihan told analysts earlier Wednesday. The comments are some of the first by a major U.S. corporation to specify the manpower and dollars spent to protect software systems from Mythos, which was released to a small group of banks, technology firms and government agencies in April.They also highlight the dual-edged nature of AI: While it can help companies save money by boosting productivity, the ability of models like Mythos to uncover and exploit decades-old software flaws has also forced firms into a costly defensive scramble. "We've got to stay ahead of them, and we've got to be mindful that the people doing the software development are the people trying to sell us the services," Moynihan said.Still, Moynihan — speaking as his company's shares slumped as much as 8% Wednesday — sought to reassure investors that the spending increase was temporary. "Once you patch, you don't have to patch as much. … The pipeline moves through," Moynihan said, adding that the bank expects remediation costs to decline over time.In other places, AI is helping to reduce expenses. Bank of America has about 130 internal AI projects, and savings from those efforts are expected to rise from $300 million this year to $700 million in 2027, Moynihan told analysts. Bank of America's head count fell by about 3,400 employees in the past year as the firm cut roughly 5% of managers, he said. It's unclear how much of that workforce reduction is attributable to AI.

schema.headline: Bank of America hired 1,000 contractors to patch software flaws exposed by Anthropic's Mythos

title: UK economy grew 0.1% in August, beating expectations
description: The U.K. economy grew by a better-than-expected 0.1% in the month to August, with production growth offsetting weak output in services and constructio
body: The U.K. economy grew by a better-than-expected 0.1% in the month to August, with production growth offsetting weak output in services and construction.Economists polled by Reuters had been expecting GDP to shrink by 0.1% between July and August. But the reading still marked a slowdown in momentum for British gross domestic product, which grew by 0.4% month-on-month in June and July. Production grew by 0.8%, the U.K.'s Office for National Statistics said in a release on Thursday, while services showed no growth and construction fell by 0.2% in August.On an annual basis, GDP grew by 2.1% in August, beating economists' expectations of 1.7%. The ONS said it marked the highest year-on-year GDP reading since August 2022. The British pound jumped 0.4% against the U.S. dollar following the release, while yields on U.K. government bonds — known as gilts — fell across the curve. The yield on the benchmark 10-year gilt was last seen trading 9 basis points lower at 5.3364%. Stock Chart IconStock chart iconU.K. gilt yieldsThe U.K., a net energy importer, is currently grappling with a cost-of-living crisis sparked by sticky inflation and surging energy costs in the wake of the Russia-Ukraine war and the Iran war. The government will unveil its closely watched Autumn Budget later this month. It's tasked with sticking to the previous government's so-called fiscal rules aimed at reigning in public debt while delivering on promises to soften the blow of surging consumer costs. Analysts said the slowdown in growth added to pressure facing U.K. finance minister John Healey as he prepares to deliver his first budget on Oct. 28. Joe Nellis, head of economic research at accountancy firm MHA, said in a note that the slowing economy will weigh on Healey's "fiscal headroom" – the amount of leeway the government has to either increase spending or cut taxes. "While continued economic growth should provide some support for tax revenues, the economy remains fragile. Rising debt interest costs have severely constrained fiscal headroom, with long-term government borrowing costs remaining exceptionally high," he said. He added that any decision to raise taxes to balance the books "carries considerable risks," threatening to weaken consumer spending, undermine confidence and discourage corporate investment. But at the same time, Nellis said, significant unfunded spending commitments could unsettle financial markets and push government borrowing costs higher.Scott Gardner, investment strategist at J.P. Morgan Personal Investing, said in a note following the ONS release that while it was positive to see the economy continuing to grow despite global challenges, the outlook for the rest of the year "remains uncertain with a tricky Autumn Budget ahead.""It's unclear right now what fiscal headroom will be left given the servicing of UK debt has increased over the last year. Many will be waiting nervously to see what the Chancellor announces," he said.Sanjay Raja, chief U.K. economist at Deutsche Bank, struck a more optimistic tone. "While we aren't seeing any dramatic course correction (so far), there are signs that the engine of the U.K. economy is slowing from its torrid pace in the first half of the year," he said, noting that consumer-facing services, construction and the IT sectors all slipped from the previous month. But while he said there would "undoubtedly… be some hiccups to come in the run up to year end" as energy prices continue to bite into household incomes and higher interest rates drag on spending and investment, Raja argued that "the U.K.'s resilience story continues.""It's hard to overstate how strong the U.K. performance has been all year," Raja said. "The U.K. economy remains the fastest growing G7 economy. What's more impressive? If you believe the HMRC jobs data, U.K. GDP growth hit 1.8% in the first eight months of the year, with 95k FEWER jobs. Who said productivity growth was dead in the U.K.?"

schema.headline: UK economy grew 0.1% in August, beating expectations

title: Nvidia, AMD, Micron fall as AI stock sell-off deepens
description: Nvidia, Micron and AMD were all down in premarket trading on Thursday, as AI stocks across the globe continued a plummet that's seen over $1 trillion
body: Nvidia, Micron and AMD were all down in premarket trading on Thursday, as AI stocks across the globe continued a plummet that's seen over $1 trillion wiped from their market caps this week. Nvidia fell 1.8%, Micron 4.4%, AMD 3.5%. Neoclouds also dropped, with CoreWeave down 5.3% and Nebius 4%. Oracle was trading at 2% lower.20 of the most valuable global AI and semiconductor stocks have shed more than $1 trillion so far this week, as interest rate hikes, AI financing and intensifying competition weighed on sentiment.A sell-off in global technology hardware stocks also deepened across Asia and Europe on Thursday.South Korean chip giant SK Hynix plunged more than 10%, while rival Samsung Electronics fell 8.73%. Other South Korean chip-related stocks also came under pressure. LG Innotek sank 8.95%, Seoul Semiconductor shed 9.28% and Samsung SDI declined 6.26%.In Japan, technology investment giant SoftBank Group tumbled 7.9%. Semiconductor testing equipment maker Advantest plunged almost 14%, while chipmaking equipment supplier Tokyo Electron lost 6.45%. Renesas Electronics declined 8%. Taiwan's TSMC, the world's largest contract chipmaker, fell 1.81%.Over in Europe, Dutch semiconductor giant ASML was last down 6.6%, Infineon Technologies shed 9.4%, and ASM International was down 9.6%, and Nokia fell 5%.Why are stocks selling off?The declines come as investors grow increasingly concerned that higher borrowing costs could weigh on the massive capital spending required to build out AI infrastructure, putting pressure on technology companies that have benefited from the AI investment boom.Concerns around global memory chip oversupply as early as 2029, as manufacturers ramp up production capacity to meet surging demand from artificial intelligence, also seem to be weighing down sentiment. China's ChangXin Memory Technologies, or CXMT, said over the weekend that it had made a breakthrough on a new architecture that could boost memory density by packing more data into a smaller space, signaling intensifying competition in the memory space. Elon Musk in an X post said China would be making "a LOT of RAM in 2028."  Chief executives of Broadcom and Intel, meanwhile, warned on Monday that financing could become a major headwind to the AI boom, with Broadcom's Hock Tan saying it could be bigger challenge to AI expansion than shortages of chips or electricity. The sell-off followed a bruising session on Wall Street Wednesday, where technology shares led broader market losses after hotter-than-expected U.S. inflation data fueled concerns that the Federal Reserve could raise interest rates further.The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite dropped 1.88% to close at 26,692.87, while the S&P 500 shed 1.11% to end at 7,718.94. The Dow Jones Industrial Average slipped 0.09%.watch nowDan Ives, tech analyst at Yorkville Ives, said the latest sell-off in AI-related stocks reflects growing concerns over the cost of financing massive infrastructure projects as U.S. Treasury yields climb above 5%, but added that underlying demand for AI computing power remains robust."Higher yields raise the cost of financing these builds, and investors are right to focus on balance sheets and contract structure, but rates are a financing question, not a demand question," Ives said in a note.The latest pullback presents a buying opportunity, Ives said, adding that the AI infrastructure boom remained in its early stages despite mounting concerns over funding costs. "What would change our view is a demand signal, not a rate signal," he said, pointing to potential cuts in hyperscaler capital expenditure plans, canceled contracts or falling GPU rental prices as warning signs.

schema.headline: Nvidia, AMD, Micron fall as AI stock sell-off deepens

title: Netflix to lay off roughly 1,000 employees, or 6% of workforce
description: The Netflix logo is displayed at a company office on May 12, 2026 in Los Angeles, California.Justin Sullivan | Getty ImagesNetflix said on Wednesday i
body: The Netflix logo is displayed at a company office on May 12, 2026 in Los Angeles, California.Justin Sullivan | Getty ImagesNetflix said on Wednesday it will lay off roughly 6% of its employees, or roughly 1,000 workers, according to a memo obtained by CNBC.The job cuts will largely impact the product, tech, legal and HR teams. "Our mission - to entertain the world - is ambitious, and delivering on it requires us to be disciplined about where we prioritize our people and resources," Netflix co-CEOs Ted Sarandos and Greg Peters wrote in the email to employees. "Our business is strong and growing, and we remain on track to deliver our full year forecast. We'll continue to invest aggressively in high impact areas to improve our service and further drive growth and innovation. "Doing that means making focused choices across the business so we can keep delivering for our members, partners, employees, and investors," the note said. Netflix said it did not have additional comments beyond the co-CEOs' memo. The company is due to report quarterly earnings on Oct. 20. The layoffs come just a few weeks after Sarandos told attendees at the Bloomberg Screentime conference that the company was "not growing as fast as I want."Netflix has faced a paradox in recent months. It continues to post solid profits and remains the biggest player in the streaming realm, but its viewing time has stagnated and the main driver of new subscriber acquisitions has been its password-sharing crackdown and the launch of a cheaper, ad-supported tier.Netflix's biggest threat has been YouTube, but looming on the horizon is Skydance. The combined entity of Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery has plans to integrate the two companies' streaming platforms, Paramount+ and HBO Max.Netflix has diversified its content in recent years, expanding into live sports, documentaries and video games in order to compete for share of consumer attention. At the same time, it's lacked the water-cooler-type hits like "Stranger Things" and "Squid Game" that previously boosted subscriber growth and viewership.And Netflix is not the only company looking to cut costs in the media space. Last month, Disney said it would lay off around 300 employees, with the majority of cuts coming from human resources and technology roles.— CNBC's Julia Boorstin and Stephen Desaulniers contributed to this report.

schema.headline: Netflix to lay off roughly 1,000 employees, or 6% of workforce

title: Ukraine to resume strikes on Russian refineries, shattering hopes of an 'energy ceasefire'
description: President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said Ukraine will resume attacks on Russian energy infrastructure after Moscow failed to uphold its end of an "energ
body: President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said Ukraine will resume attacks on Russian energy infrastructure after Moscow failed to uphold its end of an "energy ceasefire" deal proposed by President Donald Trump. "The block [on attacking refineries] is out. We're done," Zelenskyy told the Financial Times after Ukraine paused strikes on energy targets for three days at the request of Washington.On Sunday, Trump announced an "energy ceasefire" between Ukraine and Russia in an effort to put an end to the countries attacking each other's power facilities and thereby lower the price of oil and diesel ahead of the U.S. midterm elections next month. Despite Ukraine's pause, officials in Kyiv said the country has been stripped of advance warnings of incoming ballistic missiles, as Starlink connectivity services had been restricted across the country, disrupting military operations. The restrictions apply to the sister service Starshield. Serhii Beskrestnov, an adviser to Zelenskyy on defense technology, said Wednesday that SpaceX has implemented a speed limit on Starlink terminals in motion without notifying Ukrainian defense forces. "It is clear that this action cannot be a coincidence and is related to the current political situation," Beskrestnov said on Telegram.watch nowAccording to SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, the U.S. government is ultimately responsible for any curbs on Ukraine's military-grade Starlink network. "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government," he wrote on X on Wednesday.The White House and SpaceX didn't respond to CNBC's request for comment. In an interview with Piers Morgan released late Wednesday, Zelenskyy said he felt let down by Trump's recent dealings with Vladimir Putin, Russia's attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure and the apparent shutdown of Starlink. Asked whether he felt "betrayed by what has been happening," Zelenskyy answered: "Really, yes," but stressed that Ukraine's survival and its strategic relationship with the U.S. mattered more than his personal emotions. Zelenskyy said Ukraine had honored a proposed energy ceasefire for three days, refraining from both attacks and retaliation, while Russia subsequently launched a massive assault on Ukrainian energy infrastructure, including approximately 40 ballistic missiles. He said he had warned U.S. officials that Russia would violate the ceasefire and described the reported Starlink shutdown as an "absolutely crazy" move that was not consistent with the behavior expected between partners.

schema.headline: Ukraine to resume strikes on Russian refineries, shattering hopes of an 'energy ceasefire'

title: Lisa Cook lawyer doubts Trump committee's fairness as president calls her 'automatic no vote'
description: Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook and attorney Abbe Lowell leave the U.S. Supreme Court in Washington, Jan. 21, 2026.Kevin Dietsch | Getty ImagesAn a
body: Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook and attorney Abbe Lowell leave the U.S. Supreme Court in Washington, Jan. 21, 2026.Kevin Dietsch | Getty ImagesAn attorney for Lisa Cook voiced strong doubts that President Donald Trump's committee investigating mortgage fraud allegations against the Federal Reserve governor would be fair and objective.The lawyer, Abbe Lowell, said the committee is plagued by issues that undermine the appearance of the Fed's independence, including "demonstrably biased members" and "unspecified additional allegations" against Cook.Those and other issues "would have to be addressed before a hearing could occur" in the probe, Lowell wrote in a letter sent Tuesday to Will Scharf, Trump's aide and counsel. No such hearing could take place until at least December, weeks later than the initially scheduled date, Lowell insisted.The letter came three days after Trump slammed Cook as "dishonest" and griped that she was an "automatic no vote" — apparently referring to her opposition to cutting interest rates, which the president strongly desires.Cook last voted to cut rates in December 2025, siding with the majority. The Fed unanimously voted to raise rates after its most recent meeting in September."She shouldn't be in an important position," Trump said of Cook in those remarks to reporters after returning from a rally in Tennessee on Saturday.White House spokesman Matthew Middleton said in response to Lowell's letter that Trump "is performing his constitutional duty in evaluating Lisa Cook's conduct and eligibility to continue serving as a governor on the Federal Reserve.""The Constitution charges the President with ensuring that the laws are faithfully executed and that the conduct of members of the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System is above reproach," Middleton said in a statement.An in-person hearing at the White House is currently scheduled for Nov. 5, according to Trump's Oct. 7 presidential memo establishing the "committee of inquiry" into Cook.Cook's lawyers did not immediately rule out participating in that hearing, and in fact said the Fed governor "welcomes the opportunity to present the facts so she can clear her name," despite their concerns.But in Tuesday's letter, Lowell said Cook cannot attend a hearing on Nov. 5 because she "will be executing her official duties as Governor at financial and monetary policy meetings in Europe."After that, Cook will immediately start preparing for the next meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee in early December, Lowell said.The White House did not immediately respond when asked by CNBC if the scheduled hearing would be moved in light of Cook's alleged scheduling conflicts. Lowell also said he needs time to speak with Cook about issues raised by the White House's most recent correspondence, as well as to prepare her for any possible hearing, "which, because of her being in Asia on Federal Reserve duties, cannot be done until she returns.""With all of that (and court hearings I have scheduled in November), the earliest date for any hearing would need to be in December following the FOMC meeting," Lowell wrote Scharf.Trump established the three-member committee two months after reviving his long-running effort to fire Cook, an appointee of former President Joe Biden, from the central bank's board of governors.The Supreme Court in late June blocked Trump's first attempt to remove Cook, ruling that she was not given sufficient due process under federal law. But that decision did not stop Trump from trying again.Middleton said in his statement, "The President is going beyond what the Supreme Court required by offering Lisa Cook an in-person hearing that will be conducted in a fair and open process."But Lowell wrote Tuesday, "We have significant concerns regarding the objectivity and fitness of the committee," which comprises three executive branch officials, including top Trump economic aide Kevin Hassett.Hassett "already has publicly insinuated that the President has 'cause' to fire Governor Cook," Lowell noted, citing the economic advisor's comments from August 2025. Hassett in those remarks also accused Cook of "making a partisan stance contrary to the independence of the Fed" by refusing to step aside while a Justice Department investigation played out into the mortgage fraud allegations, which Cook denies.The comments suggest Hassett has already prejudged the case, Lowell told Scharf, "surely belying your assertion that the 'hearing' as proposed would be 'substantive and fair.'""A hearing with demonstrably biased members, unspecified additional allegations, and an unclear schedule for the disclosure of any additional evidence – with no explanation for why it was not previously produced – is not a process that respects the appearance or history of independence," Lowell wrote.

schema.headline: Lisa Cook lawyer doubts Trump committee's fairness as president calls her 'automatic no vote'

title: Treasury says largest U.S. banks let politics influence who received banking services
description: A sign is displayed at the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) headquarters at Constitution Center on June 1, 2025 in Washington, DC. Kevi
body: A sign is displayed at the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) headquarters at Constitution Center on June 1, 2025 in Washington, DC. Kevin Carter | Getty ImagesThe Treasury Department's Office of the Comptroller of the Currency found some of the largest banks serving the U.S. allowed political considerations, public pressure and social concerns to influence decisions about who received banking services, according to a sweeping report released Wednesday.The OCC said it reviewed the nine largest national banks under its supervision, examining nearly 100,000 complaints and about 420,000 pages of documents. It found that all nine had used "reputation risk" policies that lacked "clear," "objective" standards and could disadvantage customers because of their political or religious views or lawful business activities. "Banks should make decisions based on financial risk, not the political or social preferences of their employees or executives," Comptroller of the Currency Jonathan Gould said, according to a transcript of his in remarks Wednesday in Lexington, Kentucky.The findings may lend new regulatory weight to a grievance President Donald Trump has pressed since returning to office. Trump has repeatedly accused and sued major banks for discriminating against conservatives and has said he was personally "debanked" after the Jan. 6, 2021, Capitol insurrection, claims banks have denied.The report lands a day after the OCC and other Treasury regulators imposed more than $1.2 billion in penalties on Bank of America over separate anti-money-laundering failures. At the same time, the OCC said it is examining whether banks' efforts to comply with anti-money-laundering rules have themselves contributed to debanking. The review covered JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, Citibank, Wells Fargo, U.S. Bank, Capital One, PNC Bank, TD Bank and BMO Bank, which together held a majority of assets at OCC-supervised commercial banks when the probe began last year under a Trump executive order.The OCC stopped short of announcing fines or sanctions Wednesday, but said it is considering additional rules aimed at preventing political or religious discrimination.Among the cases it highlighted: JPMorgan subsidiary WePay closed accounts belonging to merchants selling Trump and conservative merchandise. An internal screening list included terms such as "MAGA," "Make America Great" and "America First," even though the OCC found neither WePay nor JPMorgan had formal written standards for deciding when flagged material amounted to prohibited hate or violence.JPMorgan told CNBC its policies prohibit discrimination based on political or religious views and said WePay's process "did not meet our expectations." The bank said it fixed the issue and has since shut down the business."We are not forcing these banks to serve every customer," Gould said. "Instead, banks should evaluate every customer on objective, risk-based criteria."Citi declined to comment. The other banks did not immediately respond to request for comment.The Bank Policy Institute, which represents large U.S. and foreign banks, said in a statement that the industry supports "clear and consistent standards that promote access while maintaining sound risk management," adding that political or religious beliefs should not affect access to banking services. The report also found examples cutting the other way politically. Capital One declined relationships with an abortion-rights group after noting that about 95% of its political contributions went to Democrats, and with a public education group whose political arm endorsed only Democratic candidates. It also passed on a gun-rights group over concerns that banking it could look like an endorsement.The practices extended beyond overtly political groups too, the report indicates. The OCC found restrictions affecting firearms, fossil fuels, private prisons, tobacco and cryptocurrency, and said some banks' appetite for those businesses shifted with the political climate — risking a "whipsaw" effect between administrations.All nine banks told the OCC they have since revised or consolidated policies aimed at ensuring fair access. But the regulator said none has fully acknowledged past debanking decisions or created a comprehensive program to remediate affected customers.

schema.headline: Treasury says largest U.S. banks let politics influence who received banking services

title: Trump to appeal order blocking White House from banning MS NOW, CNN and Politico
description: US President Donald Trump walks on the South Lawn of the White House before boarding Marine One in Washington, DC, US, on Tuesday, Oct. 13, 2026.Samue
body: US President Donald Trump walks on the South Lawn of the White House before boarding Marine One in Washington, DC, US, on Tuesday, Oct. 13, 2026.Samuel Corum | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesThe Department of Justice said Wednesday it is appealing a federal judge's decision to extend his order blocking the White House from enforcing its ban on MS NOW, CNN and Politico.The notice of appeal to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit came less than a day after U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly ruled that the three outlets targeted by President Donald Trump can keep their access to the White House complex.That ruling, a preliminary injunction, replaces Kelly's temporary restraining order against the ban that Trump first announced on Sept. 18. It is not a final ruling in the ongoing lawsuit that the three news outlets filed against Trump, White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, U.S. Secret Service Director Sean Curran and White House communications director Steven Cheung.Kelly, in an opinion filed Tuesday night, said the plaintiffs are likely to succeed on their claims that Trump and his co-defendants violated their First Amendment rights through unlawful retaliation and viewpoint discrimination."It is likely that Plaintiffs were selected by President Trump for revocation of their access to the White House press area because he believes their coverage of him and his administration is generally inaccurate and biased," wrote Kelly, whom Trump nominated in 2017 for his current seat."In other words, it was 'an effort to suppress the speaker's activity due to disagreement with the speaker's view' ... rather than to vindicate any other purportedly 'compelling governmental interest,' ... including maintaining professional standards for journalists or protecting national security," he wrote."Simply put, that is unlawful viewpoint discrimination," the judge wrote.Kelly was also unmoved by arguments that the decision to revoke the outlets' White House access was partly based on national security concerns "There is no evidence in the record that President Trump made the decision to revoke Plaintiffs' hard passes on national security grounds from the get-go, nor at any time has he directly stated that national security was the reason for his decision," Kelly wrote.Trump did not mention national security in his initial Truth Social post announcing the ban, nor did he do so when asked about the move later that same day, Kelly noted."All this suggests that 'national security' was merely a post-hoc justification for the decision," the judge wrote.

schema.headline: Trump to appeal order blocking White House from banning MS NOW, CNN and Politico

title: Fannie Mae sharply raises mortgage rate forecast for 2027

body: watch nowEconomists at Fannie Mae are now predicting much higher mortgage rates through the end of 2026 and into 2027. It now puts the average rate on the 30-year fixed at 7.4% for the fourth quarter of this year and 7.5% through all of next year. It previously forecast 6.8% for the fourth quarter and 6.7% for all of next year. The average rate on the 30-year fixed stood at 7.46% Tuesday, according to Mortgage News Daily, but will likely move higher today. Bond yields are rising after a hotter-than-expected inflation report. Aerial view of single family homes line the streets on April 2, 2026 in Thousand Oaks, California.Kevin Carter | Getty ImagesMortgage rates have been rising sharply since the start of September, as inflation remains stubbornly high and bond markets sell off due to several factors. The Federal Reserve also raised its benchmark rate for the first time in more than three years. Mortgage rates do not follow the Fed's rate exactly, but they do react to how the central bank sees inflation going forward. Mortgage rates loosely follow the yield on the 10-year Treasury, which has been rising sharply on higher oil prices and growing concerns in the global economy. Get Property Play directly to your inboxCNBC's Property Play with Diana Olick covers new and evolving opportunities for the real estate investor, delivered weekly to your inbox.Subscribe here to get access today.Higher rates have already put the housing market in an early deep freeze this fall. Pending sales, counted by signed contracts on existing homes, were down 8.5% in September year-over-year, according to Zillow. Mortgage demand continues to drop sharply, as buyers face higher prices and weakening affordability. Not only can fewer buyers now afford a home, but fewer can qualify for a mortgage. Fannie Mae did not respond to requests for comment on its latest forecast.

schema.headline: Fannie Mae sharply raises mortgage rate forecast for 2027

title: Iran says it’s ‘counting the moments’ until it can strike U.S. warships; Saudi Aramco facilities attacked
description: The USS Abraham Lincoln, pictured on Oct. 8 in San Diego, set a U.S. Navy record spending over 260 days consecutively at sea without a port call while
body: The USS Abraham Lincoln, pictured on Oct. 8 in San Diego, set a U.S. Navy record spending over 260 days consecutively at sea without a port call while playing a key role in Operation Epic Fury and regional maritime security operations in the Middle East. Justin Sullivan | Getty ImagesSaudi officials said Wednesday that an administrative building belonging to oil giant Saudi Aramco was targeted overnight, as the Tehran-backed Houthi militants step up their attacks on the kingdom. The strike caused a fire, but no injuries were reported at the site in the city of Dhahran on the country's eastern coast, according to a statement from the Saudi Ministry of Energy. The Houthis, a Yemen-based militia group backed by Iran, have launched a series of strikes on Saudi targets over the past week. Airport attacks in the capital city of Riyadh led to multiple fatalities, flight cancellations and property damage. Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport remains closed until Saturday.Yemen's civil war has returned to full-scale fighting between the Houthis and the country's internationally recognized government amid a wider regional escalation linked to the U.S.-Iran war.Iran 'counting the moments' until it can attack U.S. shipsIran Revolutionary Guard chief Ali Ozmaei said Wednesday that Tehran is "counting the moments" until it can sink American warships, according to Iranian state-affiliated media. "If the Americans think the Strait of Hormuz is open, let them come closer. We are impatient to sink American warships," Ozmaei reportedly said in a televised interview. "We are waiting for U.S. warships to approach the entrance to the Strait of Hormuz so we can sink them. We are counting down every moment until this happens."CNBC has reached out to the White House for comment. The Wall Street Journal reported Tuesday that the Islamic Republic has been strengthening defenses around sensitive locations like nuclear sites, and telling regional officials that Tehran will respond to any new U.S. strikes with retaliatory measures across the Middle East as it prepares its population for renewed war in the coming weeks. U.S. President Donald Trump said Thursday that American forces would not attack Iran before the midterm election, which will take place on Nov. 3.On Wednesday, reports emerged that a cargo ship caught fire and sank in the Strait of Hormuz after hitting a naval mine as it attempted to transit the waterway. CNBC was not able to independently verify the reports.  Later on Wednesday, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre — a Royal Navy-sponsored maritime security organization — said a "verified source" reported that a container ship had been struck by an "unknown projectile."In a post on X overnight, U.S. Central Command refuted Iranian claims that the strait is under Iran's control. "IRGC's navy commander has no navy. American forces and regional partners clearly control the Strait of Hormuz," Centcom said. "Just yesterday U.S. forces assisted Gulf partners in shipping more than 19 million barrels of crude oil through the strait."Correction: U.S. President Donald Trump said Thursday that American forces would not attack Iran before the midterm election. An earlier version misstated the day.

schema.headline: Iran says it’s ‘counting the moments’ until it can strike U.S. warships; Saudi Aramco facilities attacked

title: OpenAI sued by 8 states over ChatGPT safety concerns
description: A finger is poised to tap the ChatGPT app icon displayed on a smartphone screen in Creteil, France, on Oct. 1, 2026, as OpenAI begins rolling out Dots
body: A finger is poised to tap the ChatGPT app icon displayed on a smartphone screen in Creteil, France, on Oct. 1, 2026, as OpenAI begins rolling out Dots in ChatGPT, its new system of autonomous AI agents.Samuel Boivin | Nurphoto | Getty ImagesEight states filed lawsuits against OpenAI on Wednesday alleging that the artificial intelligence company's ChatGPT chatbot is an unsafe product that's harmed children and deceived parents. Iowa, Kansas, Nebraska, West Virginia, Arkansas, Arizona, Idaho and Montana have individually sued OpenAI in their own state courts, Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird said in a release. She said Iowa's lawsuit aims to "vindicate the rights of Iowans affected by OpenAI's willful, dangerous, reckless, and unlawful conduct."  "OpenAI is hurting kids and they are lying to Iowans," Bird said in a statement. "OpenAI claims ChatGPT is safe while it's giving dangerous medical advice, encouraging people to hurt others, and coaching people to commit suicide — all while pretending to be their fake friend. My lawsuit is about protecting our kids and holding OpenAI accountable under our state law."  OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said the company has built age-specific protections into its product that "many other AI products lack." He added that OpenAI is working with states to advance policies that will apply to the entire industry. "While no system can be perfect, we'll continue to work with experts to inform our work and build additional safeguards, such as the parental controls, break reminders and age-appropriate model protections that exist today," Pusateri said.OpenAI is facing mounting scrutiny over its safety and security practices, including around how the company is working to protect children. In a number of wrongful death lawsuits, ChatGPT is blamed for driving users to experience harmful delusions and, in some cases, to commit suicide. Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier also sued OpenAI in June, alleging the company knowingly released an unsafe product that could harm users.OpenAI has taken steps to enhance safety features for parents and children over the last year, and in August it launched a dedicated experience for minors called ChatGPT for Teens. That product includes a range of educational features and age-appropriate safeguards that are intended to reduce exposure to developmentally inappropriate or harmful content."Teens should be able to use AI to learn, create, and explore," OpenAI said in a release at the time. "But that access should come with protections that reflect their developmental stage, reinforce real-world relationships, and support healthy use over time."If you are having suicidal thoughts or are in distress, contact the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988 for support and assistance from a trained counselor.WATCH: Justice Department says Saudi national arrested for installing audio recording device at OpenAIwatch now

schema.headline: OpenAI sued by 8 states over ChatGPT safety concerns

title: Trump's diesel dilemma — by the numbers
description: Wholesale diesel prices have more than doubled since the beginning of 2026 through the end of September as both the war in Iran and Russia's war in Uk
body: Wholesale diesel prices have more than doubled since the beginning of 2026 through the end of September as both the war in Iran and Russia's war in Ukraine have dramatically cut global supply. Trump has insisted that the war in Ukraine is to blame for high diesel prices. On July 8, Russia banned diesel exports after Ukraine struck its refineries. In the U.S., the price of a gallon of diesel rose nearly 40% between July 6 and Sept. 22.However, the price of diesel had already jumped after the Iran war started and was still 20% above its prewar level when Russia instituted its export ban, making that tightening of supply feel that much more acute.Indeed, both conflicts have created major ripple effects across global energy markets causing major swings, sometimes daily.watch now
